newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank accounts set for revamp ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank accounts set for revamp ahead of EMU.

text.p: Germany's fiercely-independent central bank on Thursday looked set to undergo sweeping changes in its accounts after the German Finance Ministry presented plans for reform in the run-up to European Monetary Union.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a news conference in Bonn the government planned to pass a change in the Bundesbank law by the summer which would allow the central bank to raise the value of its gold and foreign exchange reserves.
The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price, a method which is normal under German book-keeping regulations.

A revaluation would effectively deliver Bonn a windfall profit, allowing it to retire old debt more quickly than otherwise. But Waigel played down this aspect of the changes, selling it instead as a technical move to prepare for the euro.
"In preparation for monetary union it is necessary to put the accounting procedures of the Bundesbank on a new basis," Waigel told a news conference in Bonn.

Waigel said that in creating a single European monetary system, the planned European Central Bank would create a set of guidelines for evaluating reserves, which he said would be "sensible and useful".
"Accordingly, the currency reserves of the Bundesbank should be valued close to market prices," he said.
In a brief two-sentence statement, the Bundesbank itself gave no specifics about the planned changes and also avoided commenting on the budgetary implications of the move.

"With respect to the principles envisioned for accounting within the European System of Central Banks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel and State Secretary Juergen Stark presented initial thoughts on changes to some definitions on accounting principles in the Bundesbank law and conducted an initial exchange of views with the members of the central bank council at the meeting," the Bundesbank statement said.
"The central bank council's discussions will be continued soon on the basis of a draft paper which will be drawn up by the German Finance Ministry," it added.

Germany, once the star candidate for EMU membership, is seeking desperately to rein in its budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product or less to make sure it qualifies fairly and squarely for entry to the euro in 1999.
The issue took on a new urgency on Thurday as experts from federal, state and local governments announced an additional shortfall of 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) in estimated 1997 tax revenues.
Germany's forecast of a 2.9 percent deficit this year is already seen as utopic by many independent analysts.
The talk of asset revaluation follows the announcement on Wednesday that Bonn is considering an earlier sale of some of its Deutsche Telekom shares.
But Waigel maintained at the news conference that neither of these moves would directly help to reduce the deficit.

Nonetheless, the revaluation would raise billions of marks in book profits. In gold alone, the Bundesbank holds 95 million ounces originally acquired at an average price of 144 marks an ounce, for a total value of 13.7 billion marks.
At the current market value of about 600 marks an ounce, it would be worth about 57 billion marks.

Waigel, who with other German officials has led a vocal campaign against the sale of a small amount of the International Monetary Fund's gold reserves, made clear in the news conference that there was no sell-off of gold planned.
"Germany will not sell one ounce of gold," he said.
